ai.definition: De novo protein design is a biotechnology process that involves designing and synthesizing entirely new proteins from scratch, without using existing natural proteins as templates.
ai.howItWorks: Involves computational modeling to predict the sequence of amino acids that will fold into a desired three-dimensional structure. This is followed by synthesis and experimental validation of the designed protein.
ai.problemSolved: Overcomes limitations in traditional protein engineering, where modifications are made to existing proteins, potentially leading to less predictable outcomes or unintended side effects.
ai.manufacturing: Requires advanced computational resources for modeling and simulation, as well as laboratory facilities for protein synthesis and characterization.
ai.buildProcess: Involves iterative cycles of design, synthesis, and testing. Computational tools predict the structure and function of designed proteins, which are then synthesized and their properties tested experimentally.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: growing market potential with increasing applications in drug discovery, materials science, and industrial biotechnology
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still evolving; current focus is on safety and efficacy of designed proteins.
ai.profitability: Uncertain, but potential for high returns in successful applications such as new drugs or industrial catalysts
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected growth in computational tools and techniques, leading to more efficient design processes and broader application areas.

glossary.def: The process of designing entirely new proteins from scratch, without using existing natural proteins as templates.
Using computer simulations to predict the structure and function of designed proteins.
The process of creating proteins in a laboratory setting, often using recombinant DNA technology.

subsystems.name: Design software
subsystems.role: generates new protein backbones and amino-acid sequences that fold into a desired shape.
parts: deep learning models trained on protein structures

subsystems.name: Structure validation
subsystems.role: predicts and experimentally verifies that a designed sequence actually folds as intended.
parts: structure prediction models such as AlphaFold

subsystems.name: Gene synthesis and expression
subsystems.role: turns a digital design into a physical protein.
parts: expression vectors and host cells (bacteria, yeast, mammalian)

subsystems.name: Screening and characterisation
subsystems.role: tests whether the designed protein performs the intended function.

subsystems.name: Iterative optimisation
subsystems.role: improves designs using experimental feedback and further computation.

subsystems.name: Application integration
subsystems.role: adapts a validated design for a specific use.

buildSteps.title: Define the target function
buildSteps.detail: State exactly what the protein must do — bind a specific surface, catalyse a reaction, or assemble into a structure — and the conditions it must survive.

buildSteps.title: Generate backbone scaffolds
buildSteps.detail: Computational methods create new protein folds, often using fragment assembly, generative diffusion models, or parametric blueprints.

buildSteps.title: Design the amino-acid sequence
buildSteps.detail: Algorithms choose residues that pack the core, satisfy hydrogen bonds, and place functional groups to perform the task.

buildSteps.title: Predict and filter structures
buildSteps.detail: Structure-prediction models and physics-based simulations check that the designed sequence folds into the intended shape without clashes.

buildSteps.title: Synthesise the gene
buildSteps.detail: The designed sequence is ordered as synthetic DNA from a commercial vendor, then cloned into an expression vector.

buildSteps.title: Express and purify the protein
buildSteps.detail: Host cells — often E. coli, yeast, or mammalian cells — produce the protein, which is then purified from the culture.

buildSteps.title: Characterise function
buildSteps.detail: Binding, catalytic activity, and stability are measured; if the design fails, the results guide a new round of computation.

buildSteps.title: Iterate and optimise
buildSteps.detail: Repeated cycles of design, testing, and redesign improve affinity, activity, or stability, sometimes using directed evolution.

buildSteps.title: Scale for application
buildSteps.detail: For commercial use, production is scaled up and the protein is formulated or integrated into a product, such as a drug or industrial enzyme.

prerequisites.why: accurate models such as AlphaFold let designers check whether a sequence will fold as intended before making it.
designs must be turned into physical genes quickly and cheaply enough to test many variants.
thousands of designs can be tested in parallel, providing the data needed to improve the algorithms.
generative models are rapidly improving but still require experimental validation and often fail on hard functions.

prerequisites.tech: Complete understanding of protein folding and function
prerequisites.why: physics-based rules are not fully solved, so designs still rely on iterative trial and error.

pathway.milestone: computational design of binders, enzymes, and immunogens in research labs; recognition with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
pathway.unlocks: a growing library of validated design rules and publicly available methods.

pathway.milestone: designed proteins enter late-stage clinical trials as therapeutics or vaccines
pathway.unlocks: regulatory experience and manufacturing know-how for designed biologics.

pathway.milestone: designed enzymes used in commercial chemical and materials production
pathway.unlocks: cleaner, more efficient industrial processes that replace harsh chemistry.

pathway.milestone: designed protein assemblies and nanomachines for medicine and materials
pathway.unlocks: programmable biological components that can be combined into complex functional systems.
